problem: Every one of the previous 50 sessions has quietly assumed a question that was never actually answered:

how does a device, a service, or a network know who a given user is in the first place? Session 20 covered Permissions, Session 21 covered Users, Session 22 covered Groups — but those sessions described how permissions and group membership work once identity already exists as a concept on a single machine.

They did not explain how FundedNext, as an organization with dozens of CEx agents, supervisors, IT staff, and systems, keeps one consistent, authoritative answer to "who is this person, what team are they on, and what should they be allowed to touch" across every laptop, server, application, and Wi-Fi login they encounter.

Without a centralized answer to that question, every single system would need its own separate list of users and passwords. Picture what that actually looks like in practice at FundedNext: a new CEx agent joins, and IT has to manually create their account on their laptop, their VPN client, their email system, their ticketing tool, their VoIP phone system, their internal KYC/refund tooling, and the Wi-Fi guest/corporate SSID authentication list — separately, one at a time, in each system. When that agent later gets promoted to team lead, every one of those systems needs to be updated individually to reflect new permissions. When they eventually leave the company, every one of those accounts needs to be found and disabled individually — and if even one is missed, a former employee retains access to something they shouldn't, which is exactly the kind of security and compliance gap that keeps auditors up at night in a financial-services-adjacent business.

This is the business problem directory services exist to solve: providing one authoritative, centrally managed, hierarchically organized store of identity and resource information that every other system can query and trust, instead of each system maintaining its own disconnected, quickly-out-of-sync copy of "who is allowed to do what."
Why this matters operationally, financially, and for compliance:
Onboarding/offboarding speed and accuracy directly affects security exposure — a centralized directory turns a dozen manual account-creation tasks into one authoritative change.
Inconsistent, siloed identity stores are a leading cause of orphaned accounts — former employees or contractors who retain access somewhere nobody remembered to check.

Auditors and regulators (relevant to a funded-trading business handling KYC data) routinely ask "show me who has access to this system and why" — a question that is nearly unanswerable without a central directory, and straightforward with one.

A single, consistent source of identity truth is also what makes single sign-on, role-based access, and centralized password policy enforcement possible at all — none of those are achievable with disconnected per-system account lists.

A directory service doesn't just store passwords — it stores the organization's answer to 'who is this, and what do they belong to,' and every other system that needs to trust identity ultimately borrows that answer rather than inventing its own.
concept: A directory service is a specialized, centralized database designed specifically to store, organize, and provide fast lookup of information about resources in a network — most commonly users, groups, computers, and organizational structure, but potentially also printers, shared folders, and applications. It is deliberately different from a general-purpose relational database (like the kind covered in Session 73, Database Servers) because directories are optimized for a very specific access pattern: read far more often than written, queried by hierarchical or attribute-based lookups rather than complex relational joins, and structured to mirror how an organization is actually organized.

The defining structural idea behind virtually every directory service is the hierarchical namespace — information is organized as a tree, not a flat list or a set of relational tables. This tree is formally called the DIT (Directory Information Tree). Each node in the tree is an entry (an object), representing something concrete like a user, a group, a computer, or a container/organizational unit used purely for organizing other entries beneath it.
Entry (Object) — a single record in the directory, such as a user or a computer, uniquely identified by its position in the tree.

Attribute — a named piece of data on an entry, such as a user's email address, phone extension, or department — directly analogous to a column in a database table, but attached per-object rather than per-table.

Schema — the set of rules defining what object classes (user, group, computer, etc.) exist and what attributes each object class is allowed or required to have — the directory's equivalent of a database schema, but typically extensible and vendor/standard-defined rather than purely custom.

Distinguished Name (DN) — the full, unique "address" of an entry within the tree, built by concatenating its name with the names of every container above it up to the root, e.g., cn=John Doe,ou=CEx,dc=fundednext,dc=local — directly analogous to a full file path in a filesystem.
Organizational Unit (OU) — a container object used purely to organize other entries into a logical structure (e.g., an OU for the CEx department, another for IT), not unlike a folder in a filesystem.

A hierarchical tree structure mirrors how most organizations already think about themselves — departments containing teams containing people — which makes it intuitive to delegate administrative control (an IT admin can be given rights over just the CEx OU without touching Finance's OU), apply policy at a specific branch of the organization, and perform fast, scoped lookups ("find everyone under the CEx branch") without scanning the entire directory.

deep: 3.1 The X.500 Legacy Modern directory services trace their conceptual roots to X.500, an ITU-T standard from the 1980s defining a comprehensive (and famously heavyweight) model for a global, hierarchical directory of "everything" — people, organizations, devices — accessible via a protocol called DAP (Directory Access Protocol) running over the OSI protocol stack rather than TCP/IP. X.500 was ambitious but impractical for most real-world deployments: DAP was complex to implement and OSI networking lost out to TCP/IP in practice, which meant a lighter-weight, TCP/IP-native alternative was needed.

3.2 LDAP — The Practical Successor LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) emerged specifically as that lighter alternative — a simplified access protocol for X.500-style directories that runs natively over TCP/IP. LDAP kept the hierarchical DIT model, distinguished names, and schema concepts from X.500, but discarded much of the OSI-specific complexity, making it dramatically easier to implement and adopt. LDAP became so dominant that today it functions as both a protocol and, informally, shorthand for the entire concept of a standards-based directory service — most enterprise directory products (Active Directory, OpenLDAP, and others covered in Session 53) are, at their core, LDAP-speaking directories.
Key LDAP concepts worth understanding at the conceptual level (LDAP itself gets a full dedicated session, Session 53):
LDAP operates over well-known ports 389 (unencrypted/StartTLS) and 636 (LDAPS, encrypted from the start of the connection).
Basic operations include Bind (authenticate to the directory), Search (query for entries matching criteria), Add/Modify/Delete (write operations), and Compare.
A search operation specifies a base DN (where in the tree to start), a scope (just that entry, one level down, or the entire subtree), and a filter (matching criteria against attributes).

3.3 Replication and Multi-Master Design A directory service serving an entire organization cannot depend on a single server — if that one server goes down, nobody anywhere can authenticate or look up anyone. Enterprise directory services solve this through replication: multiple directory servers (often geographically distributed to match office locations) each hold a copy of some or all of the directory and continuously synchronize changes with each other.
Single-master replication — one server accepts writes and pushes changes out to read-only replicas;
simpler to reason about but creates a single point of failure for writes specifically.

Multi-master replication — multiple servers can each accept writes, which are then propagated and reconciled across all replicas; more resilient but introduces the possibility of write conflicts (the same object modified differently on two servers before replication catches up) that the system must detect and resolve.

Most enterprise directory implementations favor a form of multi-master replication specifically so that a local office's directory server can keep functioning for local logins even if the WAN link to a central data center temporarily drops — a direct, practical link back to the High Availability concepts that will be covered formally in Session 79.

3.4 Schema Extensibility While the schema defines what object classes and attributes are valid, most enterprise directory products allow schema extension — adding custom attributes or object classes to support organization-specific needs (for example, a custom attribute storing an agent's CEx shift assignment or a trading-desk association). Schema changes are typically rare, carefully controlled, and forest/domain-wide in scope (foreshadowing Sessions 58–59), because a schema mistake can affect every object of that class across the entire directory.
workflow: Walking through what actually happens when a FundedNext IT administrator creates a new CEx agent's account, and later when that agent logs into their laptop, illustrates how the concepts above function together end-to-end.

1. The IT admin connects to the directory (via a management console or command-line tool) and authenticates — this itself is an LDAP Bind operation, or an equivalent authenticated session, against the directory server.

2. The admin creates a new entry under the correct OU (e.g., ou=CEx,ou=Support,dc=fundednext,dc=local), specifying the object class (typically "user") and required attributes — username, display name, and initial password among them.

3. The directory server validates the new entry against the schema — confirming the object class exists, required attributes are present, and attribute values match expected formats — and, if valid, commits the new entry and assigns it a Distinguished Name reflecting its position in the tree.

4. The new entry is replicated to other directory servers in the organization (Section 3.3), so the account becomes usable regardless of which physical directory server a login request happens to reach.

5. The admin adds the new entry as a member of one or more groups (e.g., "CEx-Agents", "VPN- Users") — group membership itself is typically stored as an attribute either on the group object (listing its members) or on the user object (listing its group memberships), depending on the directory implementation.

6. Later, when the agent sits down at their laptop and enters their username and password, the laptop's login process sends an authentication request that is ultimately resolved by querying the directory — confirming the credentials are valid and retrieving the user's group memberships, which downstream systems then use to make authorization decisions (what the agent can access) without needing their own separate copy of that information.

Notice that account creation and authentication are two distinct concerns sharing the same underlying store: the directory is the single source of truth for who exists and what they belong to, while separate authentication protocols (Kerberos, NTLM — Sessions 54–55) handle proving that a login attempt is genuinely that person, not an impostor.
enterprise: Directory services sit at a structurally central position in enterprise IT — nearly every other system either queries the directory directly or trusts something (like a token or ticket) that was ultimately derived from a directory lookup.
[Directory Service] (authoritative store of users, groups, computers, org structure) | ------------------------------------------- | | | | [Laptop/Desktop [VPN / Wi-Fi [Email / [Internal apps:
login] 802.1X auth] Collab tools] KYC/refund tooling, ticketing, etc.]
Every branch queries or trusts the SAME central directory instead of maintaining its own separate user list.
Concretely, within a FundedNext-style environment, the directory service is the foundation underneath:
Workstation and laptop logins for every CEx agent, supervisor, and IT staff member.
VPN and 802.1X wireless authentication (a direct callback to Session 50's coverage of enterprise Wi-Fi authentication tying back to Active Directory).
Email and collaboration platforms, which typically synchronize or federate identity from the central directory rather than maintaining a fully separate user list.

Internal line-of-business applications — including bespoke internal tooling like the KYC/refund/ethics web app already built for the CEx team — which, in a mature deployment, would authenticate users against the directory rather than maintaining their own separate login system.
Group Policy and centralized configuration management (foreshadowing Session 60), which applies settings based on an object's position in the directory tree.
dependencies: A directory service depends on a number of pieces of infrastructure already covered in this knowledge map being correctly in place — without them, a directory service either won't function or will function unreliably.

DNS (Session 39) — clients and servers locate directory servers (and, in Active Directory specifically, locate domain controllers for specific services) primarily through DNS records, not hardcoded IP addresses; broken DNS is one of the most common root causes of "can't reach the domain" errors.

NTP/time synchronization (foreshadowed in Session 49's mention and formally covered later) — authentication protocols built on top of directory services (Kerberos, Session 54) are highly time- sensitive, and clock drift between a client and a directory server is a classic, non-obvious cause of authentication failures.

Networking Stack and Routing (Sessions 24, 29) — directory servers must be reliably reachable across the network from every location needing to authenticate against them, including remote/branch offices.

Storage and Backup (Sessions 3, 78) — the directory database itself is a critical piece of data; its loss without backup would mean rebuilding the entire organization's identity structure from scratch.
Server hardware/virtualization (Sessions 1, 7) — directory servers are themselves servers, subject to the same hardware and virtualization considerations as any other enterprise server role.
dependents: An enormous range of enterprise capabilities depend on the directory service functioning correctly — this is precisely why directory services sit near the start of Layer 4 rather than being treated as a niche topic.
Active Directory itself (Session 52) — the specific, dominant Microsoft implementation of the directory service concept covered in this session, built on these same foundational ideas.
Kerberos and NTLM authentication (Sessions 54–55) — both rely on the directory as the authoritative store of accounts and credentials being authenticated against.
Trusts, Forests, and Domains (Sessions 57–59) — advanced multi-directory relationship concepts that only make sense once the basic single-directory model in this session is understood.
Group Policy (Session 60) — applies configuration based on directory structure and group membership.
PKI and Certificates (Sessions 61–62) — enterprise certificate issuance is frequently tied to directory identity, associating a certificate with a specific directory object.
Federation and SSO (Sessions 63–64) — extend directory-based identity outward to external/cloud applications without duplicating the identity store.
MFA and Identity Governance (Sessions 65–66) — layer additional verification and lifecycle management on top of the directory's baseline identity records.

Virtually every enterprise service covered in Layer 5 (file servers, print servers, application servers) typically authorizes access based on directory group membership rather than maintaining independent access lists.
security: Because the directory service is the authoritative source of identity for so much of the enterprise, it is also one of the highest-value targets for an attacker — compromising the directory can mean compromising the organization's entire access model in one step, which is why its security posture deserves particular care.
8.1 Why the Directory Is a High-Value Target

An attacker who compromises directory admin credentials can create new accounts, add themselves to privileged groups, or reset any user's password — effectively gaining the ability to impersonate anyone in the organization.
Because so many downstream systems trust the directory implicitly (Section 5), a directory compromise tends to cascade into a much broader compromise rather than staying contained to one system.

Directory replication (Section 3.3) means a malicious change made on one directory server can propagate automatically to every other replica in the organization, spreading the impact of a compromise geographically without additional attacker effort.

Least privilege for directory administration — very few accounts should hold full directory admin rights; delegated, scoped administrative rights (e.g., an admin who can manage only the CEx OU) limit the blast radius of any single compromised account.

Strong authentication for privileged directory accounts specifically — MFA (Session 65) on admin accounts is one of the highest-leverage single security controls an organization can apply, precisely because of how much a directory admin account can do.

Auditing and logging every write operation against the directory (new accounts, group membership changes, permission changes) — this creates the audit trail auditors and incident responders need, and is often a regulatory expectation in financial-services-adjacent environments.

Protecting replication traffic and directory server access with encryption (LDAPS rather than plaintext LDAP) and network segmentation, since directory traffic carries highly sensitive authentication data.

Regularly reviewing directory contents for stale/orphaned accounts (a former employee's account left enabled, a service account with excessive privileges nobody remembers granting) — directly connecting back to the offboarding risk described in Section 1.

Securing a directory service isn't just another item on a security checklist — because it's the root of trust for so much else, its security posture effectively sets the ceiling for how secure everything downstream can possibly be.
troubleshooting: 9.1 Common Symptoms and Likely Causes Symptom Likely Cause User can't log in anywhere, account definitely exists Directory server unreachable (DNS or network issue), or account locked/disabled/expired User can log in at one office location but not another Replication delay or failure between directory servers/sites — the change hasn't propagated yet Newly created account works for some apps but not others Downstream app hasn't yet synced/cached the new directory data, or app is querying a stale replica Group membership change doesn't seem to take effect Cached credentials/tokens on the client, or replication delay — group changes often require a fresh login/ticket to take effect Authentication fails intermittently, seemingly at random Possible clock drift between client and directory server affecting time-sensitive authentication protocols (Section 6) Directory writes succeed on one server but don't appear on others Replication conflict or a broken replication link between sites — needs direct investigation on the directory servers themselves 9.2 Diagnostic Approach 7. Confirm basic reachability to a directory server first — network connectivity and DNS resolution of directory-related service records — before assuming the problem is directory-logic-specific.
8. Check the specific account's status directly in the directory (enabled/disabled, locked, expiration date, group memberships) rather than trusting a user's description of "it's not working."
9. If the issue is location-specific, check replication status and any recent replication errors between the directory servers serving the affected location versus a working one.
10. If the issue is app-specific, determine whether that application queries the directory in real time or relies on a periodic sync/cache, and check when that sync last successfully ran.
11. For intermittent, hard-to-reproduce authentication failures, check time synchronization between the affected client and the directory server as an early, easy-to-rule-out step.

12. Review directory server logs directly for the specific authentication or write operation in question — the directory server itself usually logs a much more specific failure reason than what reaches the end user.
example: Consider a realistic scenario: FundedNext's CEx team grows from a single office to a second location in another city. Before the directory service was properly extended to the new site, IT had planned to simply have the new office's staff log into a local directory server maintained independently — effectively a second, disconnected identity store.

The problems this would create surface almost immediately: a supervisor who splits time between both offices needs two separate accounts with two separate passwords and potentially inconsistent permissions;

a departing employee at the new office requires a second, easy-to-forget offboarding step in a completely different system; and any centrally-built tooling (like the CEx team's internal KYC/refund web app) that expects to authenticate against "the" directory now has to somehow support two disconnected identity sources or, worse, maintain its own separate account list for the second office's users — reintroducing exactly the fragmentation problem described in Section 1.

The correct design instead extends the same directory service to the new location via a local, replicated directory server (Section 3.3) — new office staff get accounts in the exact same tree, under a location- or department-specific OU, replicated automatically to both sites. A single admin action (disable one account) handles offboarding regardless of which office the employee worked from, and every downstream system continues trusting one single directory rather than juggling two.
The moment an organization is tempted to stand up a second, separate identity store for convenience, it's worth pausing — that shortcut is usually how fragmented, hard-to-audit access sprawl begins.
cloud: The rise of cloud services fundamentally challenged the traditional model of one on-premises directory serving an entire organization, because cloud applications (email, CRM, ticketing, SaaS tools) live outside the corporate network the on-prem directory was designed to serve.

Cloud directory services (e.g., Microsoft Entra ID/Azure AD, Google Workspace directory, Okta Universal Directory) apply the same conceptual model covered in this session — a centralized, authoritative identity store — but hosted as a cloud service rather than an on-prem server, directly reachable by SaaS applications over the internet.

Hybrid identity is extremely common in real enterprise environments: an on-prem directory remains authoritative for internal, on-network resources, while a synchronization or federation mechanism (foreshadowed by Sessions 63–64) mirrors or federates identities to a cloud directory so that cloud/SaaS applications can authenticate against the same underlying identity without a second, disconnected account being created.

Cloud directories often adopt different underlying protocols for modern application integration — while LDAP remains common for on-prem and legacy application compatibility, cloud-native identity increasingly relies on protocols like SAML and OAuth/OpenID Connect (foreshadowed in Sessions 63–64) that were designed for web/API-based authentication rather than LDAP's network- directory-query model.

For a growing business like FundedNext, the practical trajectory is often: start with a single on-prem directory, then extend identity to the cloud via synchronization as SaaS tools are adopted, then potentially shift the cloud directory into the primary/authoritative role over time as more workloads move off-premises entirely — a gradual transition rather than an overnight switch.
automation: Directory services are one of the most automation-friendly areas of enterprise IT, precisely because so many routine tasks — account creation, group membership changes, offboarding — are repetitive, rule- based, and high-stakes if done inconsistently by hand.

Scripted account provisioning: PowerShell or Python scripts (foreshadowing Sessions 104 and 106) that create a new directory account, place it in the correct OU, and add it to the correct groups based on a standardized template (e.g., "new CEx agent" always gets the same baseline group memberships) — dramatically reducing the manual, error-prone process described in Section 1.

Automated offboarding workflows: a scripted or workflow-platform-driven process that, triggered by an HR system event, immediately disables a directory account, removes it from privileged groups, and logs the action — closing the orphaned-account security gap described in Section 8 far more reliably than a manual checklist.

Directory synchronization tooling (e.g., Azure AD Connect and similar tools) automates the hybrid identity extension described in Section 11, continuously syncing on-prem directory changes to a cloud directory without manual intervention.

Self-service tooling: much like the internal Apps Script web app already built for KYC/refund/ethics workflows, a lightweight internal tool could let team leads submit a structured "new agent" or "role change" request that triggers a reviewed, automated directory provisioning script — reducing both turnaround time and the chance of inconsistent manual setup.

Compliance/audit automation: scheduled scripts that query the directory for accounts matching risk patterns (never logged in, disabled but still group-privileged, or older than a defined age without a password reset) and generate a report for review — turning the periodic audit review described in Section 8.2 from a manual chore into a recurring automated report.
career: Directory services knowledge is one of the most consistently in-demand, cross-role skills in enterprise IT, because nearly every IT career path eventually touches identity in some form — this session marks the beginning of an entire layer of the knowledge map built specifically around that reality.

Systems Administrator / Windows Administrator roles are built heavily around directory service administration — account management, OU structure, group policy — making this session's concepts a daily, hands-on part of the job.

Identity and Access Management (IAM) is an entire specialized career track in larger organizations, focused specifically on directory design, access governance, and the broader identity lifecycle concepts this session introduces.

Security-focused roles need directory service fluency because, as Section 8 covers, the directory is one of the highest-value targets in the organization — security assessments and incident response investigations very often center on directory activity.

Help Desk and Support roles interact with directory services constantly (password resets, account lockouts, group membership questions), and understanding the underlying model (Sections 2–4) turns rote ticket-following into genuine troubleshooting capability.

For someone building broad enterprise infrastructure fluency, this session is a deliberate inflection point: Layers 1–3 covered how systems and networks function; Layer 4 begins answering who is allowed to use them — a shift from "how does the machine work" to "how does the organization control access to it," a distinction that becomes increasingly central in more senior IT and security roles.
interview: Q1: What is a directory service, and how is it different from a general relational database?

Model answer: A directory service is a specialized, hierarchically structured database optimized for storing and quickly looking up information about network resources — primarily users, groups, and computers — organized as a tree (the DIT) rather than flat relational tables. It's optimized for fast, read- heavy, attribute-based lookups rather than the complex transactional joins a relational database is built for.
Q2: What is a Distinguished Name, and why does it matter?

Model answer: A Distinguished Name (DN) is the full, unique path to an entry within the directory tree, built by concatenating the entry's name with every container above it up to the root — conceptually similar to a full file path. It matters because it's how the directory uniquely identifies and locates any given object, and it reflects the object's position within the organizational hierarchy.
Q3: Explain the relationship between X.500 and LDAP.

Model answer: X.500 was the original, comprehensive but heavyweight ITU-T standard defining the hierarchical directory model, accessed via DAP over the OSI protocol stack. LDAP emerged as a lighter- weight alternative access protocol that preserved X.500's core hierarchical/DIT concepts but ran natively over TCP/IP, making it far easier to implement — LDAP became the practical, dominant standard while pure X.500/DAP implementations largely fell out of use.
Q4: Why do enterprise directory services use replication, and what's the difference between single- master and multi-master replication?

Model answer: Replication ensures the directory remains available even if one server fails or a site loses connectivity to the rest of the network, and keeps lookups fast by placing copies close to where they're needed. Single-master replication has one server accept writes and push them to read-only replicas, creating a single point of failure for writes; multi-master replication allows multiple servers to accept writes, improving resilience but requiring conflict detection/resolution when the same object is changed on two servers before they sync.
Q5: Why is a directory service considered a particularly high-value target for attackers?

Model answer: Because so many other systems trust the directory as their authoritative source of identity and group membership, compromising the directory (especially privileged/admin accounts within it) can let an attacker impersonate any user, grant themselves access anywhere, or manipulate group memberships — turning a single compromise into a broad, cascading one rather than an isolated incident.
Q6: A new employee's account works for logging into their laptop but not for an internal web application. What would you check?

Model answer: First confirm whether the application authenticates directly against the directory in real time or relies on a periodic sync/cache — if the latter, the account may simply not have synced yet. Also check whether the account has the correct group memberships the application expects, and whether the application is pointed at the correct directory server/replica, since a replication delay could mean the app is querying a replica that hasn't received the new account yet.
misconceptions: "Directory service" and "Active Directory" mean the same thing. — False. Active Directory (Session 52) is one specific, dominant vendor implementation of the general directory service concept; OpenLDAP, FreeIPA, and various cloud directories are other implementations of the same underlying idea.

"LDAP is a product." — False. LDAP is a protocol/standard for accessing directory services, not a product itself — many different directory products, including Active Directory, speak LDAP as one of their access protocols.

"A directory service is basically just a list of usernames and passwords." — False, or at least a significant oversimplification. A directory stores rich organizational structure, group relationships, computer objects, and extensible attributes — password/credential storage is only one part of what it holds.
"Once an account is deleted, its access everywhere is immediately gone." — False in practice.

Downstream systems that cache directory data, issue long-lived tokens/tickets, or rely on periodic sync may continue to honor old access for some time after a directory-level change — a nuance directly relevant to the offboarding risk in Section 1.

"Multi-master replication means there's never a single point of failure." — Partially false. While multi-master replication removes a single point of failure for writes, poor network design (e.g., all replication traffic routed through one WAN link) can still create a practical single point of failure even with a multi-master architecture.

"Directory services are only relevant to Windows/Microsoft environments." — False. The directory service concept, and LDAP specifically, predates and extends well beyond Active Directory — Linux, macOS, network devices, and countless applications across every vendor ecosystem can and do integrate with LDAP-speaking directories.
anchors: Directory service = the organization's single phone book and org chart combined, that every other system looks up instead of keeping its own.
DIT = a tree, just like a filesystem — OUs are folders, entries are files, and a Distinguished Name is the full file path.
X.500 = the ambitious, heavyweight original blueprint. LDAP = the practical, TCP/IP-friendly version everyone actually built on.
Replication = photocopies of the phone book kept at every office, all kept in sync, so no single office losing power stops everyone else from looking someone up.
The directory is the root of trust — compromise it, and you've potentially compromised everything that trusts it, not just one system.
One person joining or leaving the company should mean one change in one place — the moment it needs multiple separate changes, the directory design has gaps.

lab: A hands-on lab suitable for a home lab or virtualized environment, using free/open-source tooling — no production access needed.

Lab Objective Stand up a basic OpenLDAP directory server, build a small DIT with organizational units and users, and perform basic LDAP queries against it to directly experience the concepts covered in this session.
Steps 13. Install OpenLDAP (or use a pre-built container image, e.g., via Docker) on a lab VM or container — this avoids needing a full Windows Server license just to explore directory concepts.
14. Define a base DN for your lab organization (e.g., dc=labcorp,dc=local) and initialize the directory with this as its root.
15. Using an LDIF file (LDAP's standard text format for defining directory entries) or a GUI tool like Apache Directory Studio, create two organizational units: ou=CEx and ou=IT.

16. Create two or three user entries under ou=CEx, giving each a distinguished name, a common name (cn), and at least one custom attribute (e.g., a department or title attribute) to see schema/attribute concepts in action.
